title: Quiz: Loss Functions — RMSE and MAE

questions.text: RMSE is defined as √(1/n Σ(yᵢ − ŷᵢ)²). Why do we square the residuals before averaging?
options: To make the result easier to interpret
To ensure residuals are positive and to penalise large errors more than small ones
To make RMSE equal to MAE
To remove the units of measurement
questions.explanation: Squaring does two things: (1) it makes all residuals non-negative so positive and negative errors do not cancel, and (2) it penalises large errors disproportionately — an error of 10 contributes 100, while an error of 1 contributes only 1. Taking the square root at the end restores the original units.

questions.text: For the same model and dataset, MAE is always greater than or equal to RMSE.
questions.explanation: It is the other way: RMSE ≥ MAE always. Squaring amplifies large residuals, so the squared average is always at least as large as the absolute average. Equality holds only when all residuals have the same absolute value.

questions.text: You suspect your dataset contains a few extreme outliers in the response variable. Which loss function should you use for fitting?
options: RMSE, because it is always the correct choice
MAE, because it treats all errors on the absolute scale and is not dominated by large residuals
Either — they always give the same fitted model
Neither — you must remove outliers before fitting
questions.explanation: MAE is more robust to outliers because it does not square residuals. A single extreme residual can inflate RMSE dramatically, pulling the fitted line toward the outlier. MAE weighs each residual proportionally to its absolute size, so one large error does not dominate.

questions.text: In a random search over 250 (β₀, β₁) pairs, the best pair found has RMSE = 1,420. You then fit lm(price ~ carat) and get RMSE = 1,330. Why is the OLS result better?
options: Random search uses MAE, not RMSE
lm() uses a closed-form formula that finds the exact global minimum of RMSE, while random search only approximates it
lm() always overfits, so its RMSE on training data is artificially low
The two methods optimise different loss functions
questions.explanation: lm() solves the normal equations analytically and finds the exact minimum of the RSS (equivalently RMSE). Random search is a stochastic approximation — it finds a good solution but is very unlikely to land exactly on the global minimum unless the search is exhaustive.

questions.text: On the heatmap of RMSE over the (β₀, β₁) space, the low-RMSE region forms a curved valley rather than a single point. What does this shape imply about the intercept and slope?
options: β₀ and β₁ are correlated — many combinations give similar RMSE because a smaller intercept can be compensated by a larger slope
The loss function is not smooth
questions.explanation: The valley shape is the signature of correlated parameters. A shift in β₀ can be partially offset by a shift in β₁ while keeping predictions (and therefore RMSE) roughly constant. This is normal for intercept-slope pairs and is why the normal equations solve the system simultaneously.

questions.text: A random search over 250 parameter pairs is guaranteed to find the global minimum of RMSE if the search range is wide enough.
questions.explanation: Random search is a probabilistic approximation. Even with a wide range, random points are unlikely to land exactly on the global minimum. As the number of parameters grows, the chance of randomly landing near the optimum decreases exponentially — this is the curse of dimensionality. Analytical methods (OLS) or gradient-based optimisers (optim) are far more efficient.
